Nova Vega stands in the Simulator Bay at Galaxy Academy. Twenty training ships rest in their cradles, sleek as silver dolphins. If she can wake her guidance core today, she joins the Founders’ Flight. If she can’t… she watches from the deck.

“Ignis,” says Orin, navigator for Bay Three. His core blooms gold.

Nova raises her wrist console. “Ignis.” A spark hiccups. Darkness.

Instructor Lyra smiles. “Starcraft listens best when it knows who’s speaking.”

Nova tries louder, slower, faster. She copies Orin’s stance. Still nothing.

She wanders to the corner “Spectra Station”: a lamp-sun, colored plates, a frosted dome, and a striped spinner. Curiosity nudges. She slides the red plate in front of the lamp. The table glows rusty. A tag reads: MARS—iron dust makes red. 

She swaps in the blue plate. The light turns ocean-deep. Tag: NEPTUNE—methane swallows red, leaves blue. Another swap: the frosted dome softens everything to pale cream. VENUS—thick clouds. She spins the striped wheel; bands drift like a stormy ribbon. JUPITER—windy belts.

Orin steps beside her. “Maybe don’t fly like me,” he says softly. “Planets don’t match, either.”

Nova studies the glowing colors. Planets don’t argue about their shades; they just show what they’re made of. Back on her drift-asteroid, she calmed skittish gliders with a three-beat tap and slow, looping paths—her version of weather.

What if they laugh?

She breathes. She chooses.

Tap, tap, tap.

Her finger draws wide, even loops on the console while she hums a quiet note. Something answers. Star-motes unfurl. The guidance sphere drinks them and swirls soft green, like bottled auroras. Thin light-rings knot a tidy bow around the yoke, approving.

Cadets ooh. Orin grins. Lyra nods. “There you are.”

That night, Nova guides the Founders’ Flight by her gentle green. Not Mars red, not Neptune blue—her color. The sky looks different in her light—edges kinder, turns full of possibility—and she likes how it makes everything, including her, look.

Hugo stands at the mossy gate of the secret village of giants. Lanterns big as bathtubs sway above him. Tonight is the Echo Festival: a great stone drum must reach the hilltop by moonrise. If it doesn’t, the song won’t carry, and the giants will think the world forgot them.

A wise owl lands on the post. “Eyes open. Ears kinder,” she hoots, then glides ahead.

Giant Grande waves. “Little friend! Help us roll the drum?” He and two giants shove. The drum crawls an inch, then slumps into a soft patch with a heavy sigh.

“Push harder!” someone booms. Dust puffs. Ropes burn palms. Nothing.

Hugo jogs around the drum and tries tiny tests. He steps in mud—his small shoe grips. Grande sets a wide foot—whoosh, he slides. Hugo tugs the thick rope; it bites his fingers. He knots a thinner cord beside it; his grip holds, while Grande’s hand barely notices it. Same tool, different result. He thinks of a school band: the tuba and the flute don’t play the same notes to make the same song.

He has a choice: keep shouting “harder”… or make a plan that fits everyone.

“Grande, use pebble pads for big feet—no slipping,” Hugo says, laying flat stones like cookies on a tray. “Giants, take the thick rope. I’ll guide with the thin line. Owl, show the driest path.” He chalks two sets of markers: wide blue circles for giant strides, small yellow dots for his. “On my count—long step for blue, quick step for yellow!”

Roll—pause—roll—easier. Up the hill they go, each using what works for their size and strength, voices moving like harmony.

At moonrise, the drum booms like friendly thunder. Giants cheer. Grande taps Hugo’s shoulder, careful and proud. Hugo smiles, warm all over, glad the village moved best when every difference had a job.

Tiko, Nuna, and Sora—three young polar bears—wake after a snowstorm. The world is white and wide. Their den is lost under fresh drifts. The wind hums over the icy desert. Tiko whispers, “We’re lost.” Nuna nods. “Let’s find our way home. Together.”

They look for clues. Sora sniffs. “I smell the sea to that side.” Nuna finds a bit of blue string caught in snow. “From our sled rope—we came this way.” Tiko sees old paw prints half-buried.

At a shiny patch they stop. “Thin ice,” Nuna says. Sora tosses a snow chunk; it splashes through. They roll three snow blocks and make a short bridge. Belly-low, they slide across, paws touching the blocks and each other.

On the other side, Nuna draws a little map in the snow with a claw. “Sea here. Big ice ridge there. Den between.” Tiko does a tiny test for direction: he sticks a twig in the snow and watches the shadow move. “The sun slides this way,” he says. “When we came, the sun was on our left. To go back, we keep it on our right.” Sora tosses a pawful of snow into the air. It blows toward long wind lines on the ground. “The wind points to the ridge,” he says.

They follow the clues. They walk in a row and take turns breaking the trail. When Sora tires, Tiko and Nuna push from behind. When Tiko’s paws sting, Nuna warms them with her fur. The wind lines grow steeper. A white mound rises—home.

They crawl inside the den, noses touching. The storm still whispers, but the den feels warm. Tiko smiles. Finding the way was hard, but their little map, the sun, the wind—and helping each other—made the path sure.

A group of young scouts hikes into the woods for their bivouac. Their packs are snug. The plan is simple: camp by Pine Creek, cook soup, read stars. But when they reach the creek, the small footbridge is gone. Water rushes fast and rough.

Jo, the junior leader, draws a quick map in the dirt. “New plan,” Jo says, pointing to a dry hill with spruce trees. The scouts nod. They climb in small steps and find a soft moss clearing.

They set camp. One scout smooths a safe fire circle on bare dirt and clears leaves a few steps away. Another fills a pot and sets it nearby “just in case.” The careful scout gathers three kinds of wood: fluffy tinder (dry grass and bark curls), thin kindling (twigs as small as pencils), and a few thumb-thick sticks for later. “Small to big,” someone says.

They try to light the pile. It smokes, then dies. “Too tight,” Jo says. “Fires need air.” They make a “tinder nest,” lay two twigs like rails, and build a tiny teepee of kindling with space between. One scout strikes the spark stick. A bright dot lands in the nest. They cup hands to block wind and whisper, “Breathe small.” The flame catches, climbs to the teepee, and begins to dance. Cause, effect. The pot goes on for soup.

The tarp hums. Stars peek out. The scouts keep the fire small and kind. They feed one stick at a time and sit on the upwind side. When the soup is warm, they share it, knees touching, voices low. The fire glows steady, and the creek’s rush sounds far away.

They didn’t sleep by the water, but they feel proud. Their plan bent, and they bent with it—together. Under the spruce, they read the first star and feel ready for tomorrow’s trail.

A group of children steps through a big paper arch into an origami world. Hills look like folded napkins. Trees are neat triangles. But nothing moves. The river is a flat blue strip. “It’s too quiet,” someone says. “Let’s wake it up.”

They find a box of colored squares. “Planes first!” Fold, crease, smooth. One child makes a sharp triangle nose. Another folds wings. A boy tosses his plane—plop. It dives and twists. He checks it and notices one wing is wider. “Not the same,” he says.

They try a “mirror match.” They fold the plane in half so the edges kiss. Left wing and right wing line up. Press—press—press along the middle crease. Toss. The plane glides farther. “Symmetry helps,” a girl smiles. They keep building. Squares become rectangles with one valley fold. Rectangles become long triangles. A child points, “Two small triangles make a diamond!”

The sky is still blank. “Maybe the planes need a sky and wind,” someone says. They shade a big sheet light blue and clip it high. They fan gently with a giant paper fan. Whoosh. A plane wobbles. “Tip the wings,” a girl says, folding tiny flaps the same on both sides. Now it circles back like a friendly bird.

They draw a dotted runway. They fold a paper bridge over the river. They add star stickers the same on each wing. With every small shape and careful match, the world seems to breathe. Trees rustle. The river shines. Planes swoop and sparkle.

At last they rest on a soft paper hill. The planes loop above in slow, happy eights. The children feel warm and proud. Their hands, shapes, and folds made the world move. “Keep flying,” they whisper, and the origami world seems to nod.

«Мост любви и понимания»

На берегу Чёрного моря жил мальчик по имени Алексей. Он приехал из России вместе с отцом, который строил новый порт недалеко от старого турецкого города.

Каждый день Алексей сидел у воды и рисовал корабли, мечтая стать архитектором.
Однажды он увидел девушку в голубом платке, которая кормила чаек. Её звали Айше. Она улыбалась так тепло, что даже волны стали тише.

Сначала они не понимали друг друга — он говорил по-русски, она по-турецки. Но с каждым днём они учили новые слова и смеялись над ошибками. Алексей научил Айше говорить «дружба», а она его — «sevgi», что по-турецки значит любовь.

Они стали настоящими друзьями. Вместе гуляли по берегу, помогали старикам в порту, мечтали о будущем. Алексей хотел строить мосты между странами, а Айше — лечить людей и приносить добро.

Но однажды Айше рассказала родителям о своём друге.
— Ты мусульманка, а он христианин, — строго сказал отец. — Он из другой страны. Мы сами подберём тебе мужа.

Айше уважала родителей, но в сердце знала, что нельзя выбирать любовь по национальности или вере.
— Папа, — сказала она, — настоящая любовь — это добро, доверие и понимание. Разве Бог не учит нас этому?

Эти слова не сразу растопили сердце отца, но они застряли в его памяти.

Прошло время. Айше и Алексей не переставали мечтать и писать друг другу письма. Они верили, что если любовь настоящая, никакие расстояния и преграды не смогут её разрушить.

Когда Айше стала взрослой, она уехала учиться медицине и стала врачом. Алексей стал архитектором и построил мост через реку — символ дружбы между двумя народами.

На открытие моста приехала Айше. Они встретились посреди моста — он с букетом ромашек, она с улыбкой, которую он помнил с юности.
Через год они поженились. Айше пригласила на свадьбу и своих родителей. Когда отец увидел, как счастлива его дочь, он понял:
— Истинная вера — это любовь и добро.

Позже у Алексея и Айше родились двое детей — Эмир и Алина. Дома они говорили и по-русски, и по-турецки, праздновали и Рождество, и Рамадан, а главное — учились уважать все культуры и людей.

Иногда вечерами семья сидела на берегу моря, и Айше говорила детям:
— Помните, мои дорогие, у людей могут быть разные языки, традиции и вера. Но если в сердце есть любовь и взаимопонимание, никакие стены не смогут вас разделить.

Алексей улыбался и добавлял:
— Вот почему мы и строим мосты — чтобы соединять, а не разделять.

И волны, лаская берег, будто шептали в такт:
— Любовь — это мост, который всегда ведёт к свету.

The Windowsill Garden Chat

Every morning, sunlight peeked through the kitchen window and warmed the little row of pots on the windowsill. There stood Aloe, tall and spiky; Pothos, with long green vines that liked to stretch; and Violet, small but proud, with purple flowers that glowed like tiny stars.

“Good morning, everyone!” said Violet, shaking a few drops of dew off her petals. “Did you all sleep well?”

“As well as a plant can,” said Aloe, with a yawn that made his spiky arms wiggle. “Though I could use a nice sip of water.”

“Same here,” sighed Pothos, her leaves drooping just a little. “I had a dream I was growing across the whole kitchen! There were shelves and chairs and—oh, it was wonderful!”

Just then, soft footsteps filled the room. It was Lila, the girl who took care of them. She wore her blue pajamas and carried a tiny watering can shaped like a duck.

“Good morning, my green buddies!” Lila said with a smile. “Time for your drink!”

She gave each pot a gentle sip. Aloe stretched happily. Pothos perked up. Violet hummed a tiny tune.

“Ahh,” sighed Aloe. “Nothing like a morning drink.”

“You always pour just right,” said Pothos. “Not too much, not too little. You must be a plant expert!”

Lila giggled. “I just listen to you,” she said. “Happy plants make a happy room.”

A warm voice called from the hallway. “Lila, breakfast is ready!” It was Mom, smiling as she came in, holding a plate of pancakes.

“Good morning, plants!” Mom said cheerfully. “You’re looking lovely today.”

Lila grinned. “Mom, they were a little thirsty, but I watered them!”

Mom nodded. “You’re taking such good care of them, honey. Did you know some plants, like Aloe, can store water in their leaves? That’s why they don’t need too much.”

Aloe puffed up proudly. “That’s right! I’m what they call a succulent! My leaves are like tiny water bottles.”

Pothos giggled. “Lucky you! I have to drink more often. My long vines get thirsty when I grow.”

Title: Tommy and the Talking Fruits

One sunny morning, four-year-old Tommy sat at the kitchen table, swinging his little legs. He looked at the big fruit bowl in front of him. It was full of bright, shiny fruits—red apples, yellow bananas, orange oranges, pink strawberries, and purple grapes.

Tommy rubbed his tummy. “Hmm,” he said. “What should I eat for breakfast?”

Suddenly, something amazing happened. The fruits began to talk!

Apple, round and red, puffed up her cheeks. “Pick me, Tommy! I’m crunchy and sweet, and I help keep you strong and healthy!”

Banana giggled and waved his peel. “Oh, pick me! I’m soft and yummy. I’ll give you lots of energy for playing and running!”

Orange rolled forward, smiling. “Don’t forget about me! I’m full of juicy vitamin C—I help you stay healthy when you get the sniffles!”

Then Strawberry bounced up with a twirl. “I may be small, but I’m full of sweetness! I make smoothies and pancakes taste extra special!”

A bunch of Grapes wiggled and laughed together. “We’re tiny, but we love to stick together—just like friends on the playground!”

Tommy’s eyes went wide. “Wow! You can all talk! But… I can only pick one fruit,” he said, scratching his head.

The fruits all started talking at once.
“Pick me!” said Apple.
“No, me!” said Banana.
“I’m the juiciest!” shouted Orange.

Tommy frowned. “You’re all so good! How can I choose?”

Just then, his mom walked into the kitchen. “Good morning, Tommy! What are you thinking about?”

“I can’t decide which fruit to eat,” said Tommy. “They all say they’re the best!”

Mom laughed and said, “Well, why not have a fruit salad? That way you can enjoy all of them together.”

Tommy’s face lit up. “That’s a great idea!”

He helped Mom slice the apple, peel the banana, cut the orange, and add the strawberries and grapes. When they were done, the bowl looked like a rainbow!

Tommy took a big spoonful and smiled. “Mmm! It’s so yummy!”

Inside the bowl, the fruits whispered happily, “See? We’re better together!”

Tommy grinned. “You’re right! When I eat you, I feel happy and strong—just like you!”

From that day on, Tommy always asked for a colorful bowl of fruits for breakfast. Because he knew the secret the fruits had taught him:

You are what you eat—and when you eat happy, healthy fruits, you feel happy and healthy too!

The End. 🍎🍌🍊🍓🍇

Title: Santa’s Big Gift Meeting

It was a snowy morning at the North Pole. The North Pole is a very, very cold place at the top of the world, where the snow never melts and the stars sparkle like diamonds in the sky. Snowflakes twirled like tiny dancers, and Santa’s workshop glowed with warm golden light. Inside, Santa sat at his big round table with all his helpers — the elves, Mrs. Claus, and the reindeer peeking through the frosty window.

“Ho ho ho!” Santa laughed, his belly jiggling. “Christmas is almost here! We must decide what gifts to make for all the good boys and girls!”

The elves cheered. “Let’s make shiny trains!” said Tinker the Toymaker.

“Cuddly teddy bears!” shouted Sparkle, hugging a fluffy bear tight.

“Don’t forget bikes!” said Rudy the reindeer, shaking his antlers. “Kids love to ride fast!”

Santa rubbed his chin. “Those are wonderful ideas. But what gifts will make the children happiest?”

The workshop went quiet until a soft voice spoke. It was Pip, the tiniest elf, holding a box of ribbons. “Santa,” he said, “maybe it’s not just the toys that make them happy. Maybe it’s knowing someone worked hard to make something special just for them.”

Santa’s eyes twinkled. “Ho ho! That’s very wise, little Pip. Every gift carries love from the hands that made it.”

So the helpers got to work. The elves painted trains and dressed teddy bears in tiny scarves. Mrs. Claus baked cookies for everyone and filled the air with the smell of cinnamon. The reindeer practiced flying high through the snowy sky, their bells jingling bright.

At last, everything was ready. Santa’s sleigh sparkled under the moonlight, piled high with colorful presents. “Thank you, my friends,” Santa said kindly. “Because of your love and hard work, every child will feel the magic of Christmas.”

“Ho ho ho! Time to deliver joy!” he called, as the reindeer leapt into the sky.

They flew over mountains and sleepy towns. Below, soft lights twinkled in windows. Santa landed quietly on rooftops, and with a wink, he slid down chimneys, leaving gifts under twinkling trees — a train here, a bear there, a shiny red bike leaning near the stockings.

In one cozy home, a little girl woke up just as Santa tiptoed out. She gasped softly when she saw the gifts. “Oh, thank you, Santa,” she whispered. She hugged her teddy tight, not knowing how many elves had worked so hard to make it.

Back at the North Pole, Santa and his helpers watched the stars fade into dawn. “The children will wake soon,” said Pip with a smile.

Santa nodded. “Yes, and they’ll feel the love we put in every gift. That’s the best part of Christmas.”

The End

Lesson:
Every gift is special because of the love and effort behind it. When we appreciate what others do for us, we spread joy — just like Santa and his helpers do every Christmas.

Dusty rides his pony, Rusty, on the wide, grassy prairie. He holds his new, twirly lasso. In the distance, he sees what he is looking for: a family of wild horses. Their coats shine like copper pennies in the sun. A beautiful white stallion leads them. "Wow," Dusty whispers. "I'm a real cowboy. I'm going to catch that amazing horse!"

Dusty kicks Rusty's sides. "Yee-haw!" he shouts, riding closer. He swings his lasso. But the wild horses are like the wind. Whoosh! They flick their tails and race over the hill. Dusty sees their big, scared eyes as they run. He stops, feeling grumpy and out of breath.

He thinks. "Maybe they just need food." He finds their watering hole and leaves a big pile of sweet hay from his saddlebag. He hides behind a big, gray rock.

The horses come back. They drink the cool water. The white stallion looks at the hay. He sniffs it, then nudges his family away. He leads them to a patch of fresh, green prairie grass, and they all start to eat. Dusty sees they know just where to find their own food.

Dusty watches them. The stallion gently bumps his head against a little, long-legged foal. The whole family looks so happy and safe, running together in their big, open home.

Dusty's heart feels warm. He suddenly understands. They don't want his hay or his rope. The best way to help them is to let them be wild and free.

Dusty quietly coils his lasso and hangs it on his saddle. He smiles. "This is your home," he whispers. He turns Rusty and rides away, happy just knowing the wild horses are safe.

In the bright blue kingdom of dolphins, Marina the dolphin swims in the royal coral courtyard. Colorful fish slip between coral branches, and sea grass waves like a green forest. Marina likes to watch how every creature has a place and a job in this underwater city.

High above, a round hole in the water’s ceiling lets sunlight pour down. One day, tiny glowing seashells begin to drift through the hole. They sparkle as they sink, like pieces of sunlight.

“Amazing,” Marina says. “If I collect these shells, I will be the shiniest dolphin in the whole kingdom.”

She finds a big clam shell and uses it as a basket. As she chases the glowing shells, she notices how light helps the sea grass grow and gives shy fish a safe place to hide. Still, she thinks, I want all the glow for me.

Marina zooms and flips, catching shell after shell. Sometimes she bumps a coral branch and sees a crab wave its claws in surprise. Sometimes she stirs up sand, and tiny worms wriggle out. She giggles, but she keeps filling her basket.

Soon her basket shines so brightly that the courtyard around her looks dim. The sea grass meadow is a blur of shadow, and the path between coral towers is hard to see.

“Marina?” whispers a small seahorse. “I can’t find my way home. It’s too dark.”

“My little ones are scared,” says Turtle from behind a rock. “They cannot see our cave.”

Marina hugs her glowing basket. Then she looks at the worried eyes around her and at the shadowy coral that so many animals share.

Gently, she tilts her basket.

The shells float out and spread across the courtyard, resting on coral, stones, and sea grass. Soft light fills every corner. Fish find hiding spots, seahorse sees the path, Turtle’s babies swim out, laughing.

Marina keeps one small shell on her necklace, but as her friends thank her, she feels a deep, gentle brightness inside—like the whole ocean is glowing in her heart.

Coral is a young villager who lives in an ocean village called Shellshore. The houses stand on wooden stilts above the bright blue water. Every morning, Coral sits on the dock and watches colorful fish swim between the coral below.

One morning, when Coral skips down to the dock, she stops. The water looks dull and messy. A plastic bag floats near the posts. Old bottles and food wrappers drift between the rocks. A gull pecks at a cracked cup.

“If we keep doing this,” Coral whispers, “the ocean will grow sick.”

She decides to help. First, Coral uses a fishing net to scoop trash into a bucket. The bucket fills quickly, but more junk keeps bumping against the dock. Her arms grow tired. She sighs. “I can’t do this alone. And some of this can be used again.”

Coral runs along the wooden walkway and knocks on doors. “Villagers of Shellshore!” she calls. “The ocean is our neighbor. It needs us. Come help clean it before it gets sick. We can also learn how to recycle!”

Soon children and grown-ups come with buckets and old baskets. Together they pull out bags, bottles, and broken toys. On the pier, Coral helps everyone sort the trash. “Soft plastic bags go in this bin,” she says. “Glass bottles go in this one. Clean cans go here. Things we really can’t use go in the last bin.”

They rinse bottles with seawater and stack cans neatly. A small pile of clean caps and pretty bits becomes “art pieces” for future crafts.

By sunset, the water around Shellshore is clear again. Fish dart through the coral. The villagers sit with Coral on the dock, feet dangling above the gentle waves. Coral feels tired, but proud and calm. Now the whole village knows that recycling and cleaning up can keep their ocean friend safe and sparkling.

Mina is a young girl who loves the small garden behind her house.
Bright marigolds, shy violets, and climbing green beans grow there, like quiet friends she sees every day.

One hot, golden morning, Mina’s mom says, “I must go to town. The sun will be strong today. Please take care of the garden while I’m gone.”

Mina’s heart jumps. “All by myself?” she asks.

Her mom nods. “You can do it. The plants need their daily care, just like you need breakfast and toothbrushing.” Then she leaves through the gate.

The garden feels still. The soil is dry and cracked. The marigolds droop. Mina decides to make a “garden morning routine,” the way she has her own.

First, she fills her small watering can. “Water time,” she tells the plants, giving each one a careful drink. The beans get long, slow streams. The violets get soft little sprinkles. She notices how the soil drinks the water, turning darker and cooler.

Next, she gently pulls tiny weeds, like tidying a messy room. She lines up her tools on a flat rock—watering can, trowel, and a small brush to dust soil off the leaves. “Everything in its place,” she says.

Then Mina finds an old sheet and two sticks. She makes a shade tent over the weakest flowers. “Rest time, like my quiet time after school,” she whispers.
